newsitem.title: USA: Treasuries end higher after fresh supply dose.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries end higher after fresh supply dose.

text.p: Prices of U.S. Treasury securities posted their first gains of the week Wednesday, ending higher across the yield curve after digesting another fresh dose of supply.

Relieved that the Treasury's sale of $12.5 billion in five-year notes was out of the way, prices staged a modest rally in the afternoon and moved into positive territory after two consecutive days of losses.
Talk of Federal Reserve buying in the five-year sector was also seen bolstering prices in the aftermath of the auction.

"Supply is out of the way, the auction came pretty much right where it was expected to come and we saw some relief trade," said Michael McClure, head of government bond trading at Zions First National Bank Capital Markets. "People are going back to their bullish ways."

The benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year bond was up 10/32 at 98-31/32 to yield 6.83 percent in late Wednesday trading vs. 6.85 percent on Tuesday. The two-year note also advanced, rising 1/32 to 99-28/32 and yielding 5.94 percent in late dealings.

Without any economic data to focus on, the market relied on supply again on Wednesday for much of its direction. Market analysts characterised the Treasury's five-year note sale as largely in line with expectations.
They noted, however, that the market appeared better prepared for the supply than it had been on Tuesday, when the Treasury's two-year note sale gave way to widespread selling.

The Treasury sold the five-year notes at a high yield of 6.325 percent, awarding 55 percent of the bids at the high rate. Of the $28.181 billion in bids received, $326 million were non-competitive offers.
The bid-to-cover ratio, a gauge of demand for the issue, came in at a slightly soft 2.33.
"It was really plain vanilla," said John Canavan, treasury market analyst at Stone & McCarthy Research Associates Inc. "There was nothing particularly exciting about it one way or the other."

Having digested over $30 billion in supply in a two-day span, the market breathed a sigh of relief once the auction passed. Talk that the Federal Reserve was buying five-year notes on behalf of foreign central banks helped reinforce the price gains, analysts said.
Dealers could not confirm the Fed purchases, but said the behaviour of the market and the widespread nature of the reports suggested the central bank may have indeed been active.

With supply out of the way, Treasuries are now expected to begin looking ahead to Friday's report on September durable goods orders and next week's busy calendar, which includes key October employment figures.
Economists said the market was hopeful the upcoming numbers would be supportive, but hesitant about betting on further price gains.
"There are still a lot more hurdles ahead," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International. "Most people are still expecting friendly numbers, but no one is making a strong play yet."
In the corporate market, cable and media debt dominated trade, but the sector marred by further widening in TCI Communications paper, traders said.

The slide in TCI debt has slowed, but issues still widened in the 5-to-10-basis-point range into the close. TCI debt has widened by more than 40 basis points since the Standard & Poor's rating agency late Friday said it might downgrade the credit to junk status.
TCI's 6-7/8 percent debt due 2006 was bid 7 basis points wider at 227 basis points near the close. The notes widened 15 basis points on Tuesday.

Elsewhere, Viacom Inc. debt was softer for the second consecutive session following news it may pay MCA $1.45 billion and exchange its 50 percent interest in the SciFi Channel for complete control of the USA Network.

Viacom debt due 2005 closed at 190 basis point bid, 185 basis point offer. Spreads firmed early on Wednesday after an S&P ratings affirmation late on Tuesday, one trader said, but the paper soon retreated to wider levels.
U.S. municipal bonds recovered to flat from early losses of up to 3/4 of a point after the Treasury market rebounded, but traders questioned how much room dealers had left for new issues.

With a mammoth $4.8 billion of new municipal bonds expected to be sold this week, dealers still appeared to be holding a number of these issues themselves. This could cut their buying interest for next week's new offerings, which includes some very large issues, though the total is less.

For example, the calender includes $910 million of New York State Dormitory Authority revenue bonds, nearly $600 million of New York State Urban Development bonds, and almost $450 million of North Carolina issues.
